questions.title: How can one spouse validly consent to police entry into a shared home when the other spouse is inside and never asked?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the third-party consent part of this opinion. The court says Lisa could consent to the officers entering the home she shared with Coleman, even though Coleman was also a resident and was physically present somewhere inside the house. I thought there were limits on one co-occupant overriding another co-occupant's Fourth Amendment interests. Is the key point that Coleman was not at the door objecting, so this is different from a case like Georgia v. Randolph? In other words, when does a present-but-not-consulted co-occupant block consent, and when does the consenting spouse's authority control?

questions.title: Does an initial refusal followed by a later 'okay' still count as voluntary consent, or do repeated requests make it coercive?
questions.question_body: Lisa first said, 'I'd prefer you not' when Officer Kizer asked to come in, but a little later she said 'Okay' after he raised the issue again. The Seventh Circuit treats the earlier refusal as evidence that she was capable of saying no, which supports voluntariness. But couldn't the opposite inference also be drawn—that the officer kept asking until he got the answer he wanted? How do courts evaluate whether a later consent is genuinely voluntary after an earlier refusal, especially in a tense domestic-violence situation?

questions.title: When does language like 'we almost need to come inside' become an unconstitutional claim of authority rather than a request for consent?
questions.question_body: The defendant argued that Officer Kizer's statement—'I'm sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure of that'—was coercive. I'm having trouble understanding where the line is between an officer expressing urgency and an officer effectively telling the occupant that entry is going to happen regardless of consent. Under Bumper, consent is invalid if it's just acquiescence to a claim of lawful authority. So why did the court treat 'need to come inside' as compatible with voluntary consent here? Is the difference mainly tone and context, or is there a more specific doctrinal test?

questions.title: Did the officer 'cracking the door' and calling into the house before consent already amount to a Fourth Amendment entry or search?
questions.question_body: One factual detail threw me off: after Lisa said she needed to get her shoes and did not come back outside for a while, Officer Kizer 'cracked the door' and called into the house asking if she was okay. The opinion then focuses on the later consent as the justification for entry. But wasn't opening the door at least arguably a physical intrusion into the home before consent was given? If so, why isn't that analyzed as a separate Fourth Amendment issue? Is it because the defendant did not press that point, because it was too minimal to count as an entry, or because officer-safety/community-caretaking concerns would justify it?

questions.title: How broad was Lisa's consent to enter—did it really authorize a sweep of the home and questioning of everyone inside?
questions.question_body: The court says the officers stayed within the scope of consent because their stated purpose was to check on the children and make sure Coleman was not a danger. I understand that this would allow them to go to the children's bedroom, but the opinion seems to say it also allowed them to scan the home, locate Coleman in another bedroom, and ask the children questions about what happened. Under the 'objective reasonableness' test from Florida v. Jimeno, how do courts decide what a reasonable person would think was included in consent for a welfare check? At what point would the officers have exceeded the scope and needed either separate consent, exigent circumstances, or a warrant?

questions.title: Why is the appellate standard 'clear error' for voluntariness and scope of consent, especially when the interaction was captured on body camera?
questions.question_body: The Seventh Circuit says it reviews the district court's findings on voluntary consent and scope for clear error, and it also emphasizes that the key facts came from body-camera footage. I'm confused about how much deference is really owed when the appellate judges can watch the same video themselves. Shouldn't video reduce the need to defer to trial-level factfinding? Also, the district court adopted a magistrate judge's recommendation—does that affect the level of appellate deference at all?

questions.title: How was Coleman able to plead guilty and still appeal the suppression ruling?
questions.question_body: Procedurally, the opinion says Coleman pled guilty 'while reserving his right on appeal to challenge the suppression ruling.' I thought a guilty plea usually waives most prior issues. Is this a Rule 11(a)(2) conditional plea, and if so, what exactly has to happen for a suppression issue to remain appealable after a guilty plea? Also, if he had entered an ordinary guilty plea without explicitly reserving the issue, would this Fourth Amendment argument have been lost?
